title: Chapter 5.4 — Solving Special Systems of Linear Equations
presenterNotes: Start by reviewing the three possibilities for linear systems. Use the analogy of roads: crossing (one solution), parallel (no solution), same road (infinitely many).
Emphasize that slope‑intercept form is the fastest way to classify a system. Practice quickly rearranging equations into $y = mx + b$.
When solving algebraically, the moment variables cancel, stop and evaluate the remaining statement. A true statement means same line; a false one means parallel.
In real‑life problems, always discuss the domain. Even with infinitely many solutions algebraically, the context may restrict the answers (e.g., positive lengths).

steps: Find the slope of the first line: $m_1 = 1$.
Rewrite the second equation in slope‑intercept form: $y = -x + 2$. The slope $m_2 = -1$.
Because $1 \ne -1$, the slopes are different, so the system has exactly one solution.
examples.title: A – Identifying One Solution from Equations
examples.prompt: Without graphing, determine how many solutions the system has: $y = x + 2$ and $x + y = 2$.

examples.title: B – Why Different Slopes Guarantee One Solution
steps: If slopes are different, the lines are not parallel.
Non‑parallel lines in a plane must intersect at exactly one point.
That intersection point gives the unique solution to the system.
examples.prompt: Explain why a system whose equations have different slopes must have exactly one solution.
examples.peerPrompt: Discuss with a partner: Picture two lines with different steepnesses. Can they ever be parallel? Can they be the same line?

examples.prompt: Solve the system $y = x + 2$ and $x + y = 2$ by any method.
examples.title: C – Solve a One‑Solution System
steps: Then $y = 0 + 2 = 2$. Solution: $(0, 2)$.

confusionCorner.body: If the slopes are the same but the $y$‑intercepts differ, the lines are [[imp:parallel]]. They never intersect, so the system has no solution. Don't confuse this with having one solution.

discoveryHook.scenario: When two roads cross, there is exactly one spot where they meet. In a system of linear equations, if the lines have different slopes, they will always intersect at exactly one point. That unique intersection is the one and only solution!

Any method can be used to find it.
formulaCard.title: One Solution System

explanation: A system of linear equations can have [[imp:one solution]] when the graphs intersect at a single point.
This happens when the lines have [[imp:different slopes]].
The solution is the ordered pair $(x, y)$ where the lines cross.
You can solve these systems by graphing, substitution, or elimination—the answer will be the same.

steps: Substitute $2x - 5$ for $y$ in the first equation: $2x - 5 = 2x + 1$.
Subtract $2x$ from both sides: $-5 = 1$, which is false.
There is no value of $x$ that makes this true. The system has no solution.

steps: Rewrite in slope‑intercept form: $y = -x + 3$ and $y = -x + 2$.
Both have slope $-1$, but different $y$-intercepts ($3$ and $2$).
Same slope → parallel lines → no intersection → no solution.

steps: Subtract the second equation from the first: $(3x-3x) + (-y - (-y)) = 6 - (-3)$ → $0 = 9$.
The statement $0 = 9$ is false. The system has no solution.

formulaCard.title: No Solution System
notes: Elimination or substitution yields a false equation.

explanation: A system has [[imp:no solution]] when the graphs are parallel lines.
Parallel lines have the [[imp:same slope]] but [[imp:different y-intercepts]].
Algebraically, solving leads to a false statement (e.g., $0 = 5$).
This means there is no ordered pair that satisfies both equations simultaneously.

confusionCorner.title: Don't Call It 'No Points'
confusionCorner.body: A system with no solution doesn't mean there are no points anywhere—it means there is [[imp:no common point]] that works for both equations. Each line individually has infinitely many points.

teacherCues: Graph y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x - 5 on the same grid. Ask: 'Where do these lines meet?'
Write the system and show that substitution gives a false statement like -5 = 1.
blocks.title: Systems with No Solution

examples.title: A – Solve and See Infinitely Many
steps: Multiply the first equation by $-2$: $4x - 2y = -6$.
Add to the second: $(4x-4x) + (-2y+2y) = -6+6$ → $0 = 0$.
The true statement means the equations are the same line — infinitely many solutions.

examples.peerPrompt: Discuss with a partner: What happens if you divide the second equation by 2?
examples.prompt: Explain why $x + y = 3$ and $2x + 2y = 6$ have infinitely many solutions.
steps: Divide $2x + 2y = 6$ by 2: you get $x + y = 3$.
This is exactly the first equation, so they represent the same line.
Every point on $x + y = 3$ is a solution to both.
examples.title: B – Recognizing Equivalent Equations

steps: Substitute $y$ into the second: $2x + 2(-x + 3) = 6$ → $2x - 2x + 6 = 6$ → $6 = 6$.
The statement is always true — infinitely many solutions.
examples.title: C – Substitution to Reveal Infinitely Many

blocks.title: Systems with Infinitely Many Solutions

formulaCard.title: Infinitely Many Solutions System
notes: The equations represent the same line.

explanation: A system has [[imp:infinitely many solutions]] when the graphs are the same line.
This happens when the equations are [[imp:equivalent]] — they have the same slope and the same $y$-intercept.
Algebraically, solving leads to a true statement like $0 = 0$.
Any ordered pair that satisfies one equation automatically satisfies the other.

confusionCorner.title: Infinitely Many ≠ All Points
confusionCorner.body: Infinitely many solutions means every point on the shared line is a solution. It does [[imp:not]] mean every point in the coordinate plane is a solution. The solutions lie on a specific line.

discoveryHook.scenario: If two equations are just different versions of the same line—like a sentence rewritten in different words—they describe the same path. Every point on that line is a solution to both equations, giving you infinitely many solutions!

examples.title: A – Classify by Slopes and Intercepts
examples.prompt: Without solving, determine the number of solutions for $y = -6x - 8$ and $12x + 2y = -6$.
steps: Rewrite the second equation: $2y = -12x - 6$ → $y = -6x - 3$.
Both have slope $-6$. First $y$-intercept is $-8$, second is $-3$.
Same slope, different intercepts → no solution.

examples.title: B – Classify with Different Slopes
steps: Solve for $y$: first → $y = -\frac{4}{3}x + 9$; second → $y = \frac{4}{3}x + 9$.
Slopes are $-\frac{4}{3}$ and $\frac{4}{3}$ — different.
Different slopes → exactly one solution.
examples.prompt: Determine the number of solutions for $4x + 3y = 27$ and $4x - 3y = -27$.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: How can you quickly find the slopes without fully solving for $y$?

examples.prompt: Determine the number of solutions for $y = 7x + 13$ and $-21x + 3y = 39$.
examples.title: C – Equivalent Equations
steps: Rewrite the second: $3y = 21x + 39$ → $y = 7x + 13$.
Both equations are identical. Same slope and intercept → infinitely many solutions.

confusionCorner.body: To compare slopes and intercepts, equations [[imp:must]] be in slope‑intercept form. An equation like $2x + 3y = 6$ needs to be rewritten before you can read $m$ and $b$.
confusionCorner.title: Must Be in y = mx + b First

teacherCues: Draw three quick graphs on the board: intersecting lines, parallel lines, coincident lines. Ask: 'Which is which in terms of solutions?'
Summarize the slope/intercept conditions for each case in a table.

notes: Fastest way to classify a system.
formulaCard.title: Deciding Without Solving
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Write both as } y = mx + b \text{, then compare } m \text{ and } b. $$

explanation: You can determine the number of solutions by comparing slopes ($m$) and $y$-intercepts ($b$).
[[imp:One solution]]: $m_1 \ne m_2$.
[[imp:No solution]]: $m_1 = m_2$ and $b_1 \ne b_2$.
[[imp:Infinitely many]]: $m_1 = m_2$ and $b_1 = b_2$.
These rules work for any linear equations after rewriting in slope‑intercept form.

discoveryHook.scenario: Just like Goldilocks, systems can have exactly one, none, or infinitely many solutions. By looking at the slopes and y-intercepts, you can tell at a glance which situation you're dealing with—no solving required!

confusionCorner.title: Context Limits Solutions
confusionCorner.body: Even if a system has infinitely many solutions algebraically, real‑world constraints (like $x > 0$, $y > 0$, whole numbers) may limit the acceptable answers. Always apply the context.

explanation: The blueprint for special systems: [[imp:Understand]] – Write the equations and identify slopes/intercepts or plan a solving method.
[[imp:Solve]] – Use substitution or elimination. If variables cancel, note the resulting statement.

[[imp:Conclude]] – True statement → infinitely many solutions (the same line). False statement → no solution (parallel lines). In context, interpret what this means (e.g., infinitely many possible dimensions, or impossible conditions).

rows.1: Write equations; note if they look proportional.

notes: Always check the context for domain restrictions.
If variables don't cancel, you have one solution.
formulaCard.title: Blueprint Decision

examples.prompt: The trapezoid has sides $2x, 4x, 6y, 6y$ and perimeter $48$. The rectangle has sides $9x, 9x, 18y, 18y$ and perimeter $144$. Write and solve the system.
examples.title: A – Perimeter Problem
steps: Understand: Trapezoid perimeter: $2x+4x+6y+6y=48$ → $6x+12y=48$. Rectangle: $9x+9x+18y+18y=144$ → $18x+36y=144$.
Solve: Multiply first by $-3$: $-18x-36y=-144$. Add to second: $0=0$.
Conclude: Infinitely many solutions. In context, $x$ and $y$ must be positive. Many possible dimensions satisfy both perimeters.

examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why might a system with proportional coefficients lead to a special solution?
steps: Let $x$ = price per cup fruit, $y$ = price per cup almonds.
System: $3x + 4y = 9$ and $4.5x + 6y = 6$? Actually the image likely shows costs: small $9, large $6. But let's suppose small $9, large $6. Then equations: $3x+4y=9$, $4.5x+6y=6$.

Notice $4.5/3 = 1.5$ and $6/4 = 1.5$. If the cost ratio also matched $9/6 = 1.5$, they'd be proportional and have infinite solutions. But $9/6 = 1.5$ actually! So they are proportional! That would mean infinite solutions or no solution depending on constant. $4.5x+6y = 1.5(3x+4y) = 1.5*9 = 13.5$, but the equation says it equals $6$. So $13.5 = 6$? Actually the book says large bag $6? That seems cheap. Anyway, the concept: if proportional coefficients but different constant, no solution.
examples.title: B – Trail Mix Bags
examples.prompt: A small bag of trail mix (3 cups fruit, 4 cups almonds) costs $9. A large bag (4.5 cups fruit, 6 cups almonds) costs $6? No, $9 and $6? Let's use consistent data from the exercise: small: 3 fruit + 4 almond = $9? Actually exercise says small bag $9, large bag $6? Wait, the exercise 25 says small bag contains 3 cups dried fruit and 4 cups almonds, large bag 4.5 cups fruit and 6 cups almonds, costs? It says 'Write and solve...' but doesn't give costs? Actually the image shows $9 and $6 next to the bags. So small bag $9, large bag $6. Wait, that seems reversed. Anyway, use the idea: if the equations are proportional, infinite or no solution.
Team A goes 6 mph and is 2 miles ahead. Team B goes 6 mph. Write a system and determine if Team B catches up.
steps: Let $y$ = distance from start, $x$ = time in hours.
Team A: $y = 6x + 2$. Team B: $y = 6x$.
Both have slope 6. Different intercepts → parallel lines → no solution.
Team B never catches Team A because they travel at the same speed.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Solving Special Systems

discoveryHook.scenario: When you encounter a system that simplifies to $0 = 0$ or $0 = 5$, you've found a special system. The blueprint helps you pause and understand what that means—instead of thinking you made a mistake, you'll recognize a system with infinitely many or no solutions.
